title: 5.2 Applications: Work & Enthalpy
synopsis: Many reactions produce gases that can push a piston (work) or release heat. This section puts numbers on both. It derives the work formulas for different processes, introduces the new state function enthalpy (H), separates extensive and intensive properties, and defines heat capacity along with Cp − CV = R.

children.title: 5.2.1 Work (Pressure–Volume Work)
children.synopsis: Only mechanical (pressure–volume) work is considered. Picture one mole of ideal gas in a cylinder with a frictionless piston. The work depends on how the external pressure changes during the process.

children.title: Single-step Work: w = −pₑₓΔV
children.synopsis:
A constant external pressure pex compresses the gas in one step. The piston (area A) moves a distance l, so ΔV = l × A = Vf − Vi.

Force = pex · A, so work = force × distance = pex · A · l. Adding the sign:

w = −pexΔV = −pex(Vf − Vi) (Eq. 5.2)

The minus sign makes the convention work out. In compression ΔV is negative, so w comes out positive (work done on the system). In expansion ΔV is positive, so w is negative.

On a p–V graph, the work equals the shaded rectangle under the constant pex line.
traps: Always use EXTERNAL pressure, not gas pressure, for irreversible work.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands from 2 L to 5 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. The work done (1 L atm = 101.3 J) is about:
questions.e: w = −p_ex ΔV = −1 × (5 − 2) = −3 L atm ≈ −304 J. It is negative because the gas does work on the surroundings.

questions.q: During compression of a gas, the sign of work (IUPAC) is positive because:
o: ΔV is negative, and w = −p_ex ΔV
questions.e: In compression V_f < V_i, so ΔV < 0 and w = −p_ex ΔV > 0.

children.title: Multi-step & Reversible Processes
children.synopsis:
Finite steps: if pex changes in several steps, total work = −Σ pΔV, a staircase of rectangles on the p–V graph.

Infinite steps: if pex is always only infinitesimally greater than the gas pressure (pex = pin + dp for compression, pin − dp for expansion), then

w = −∫ pex dV (Eq. 5.3)

Such a process is reversible. At any moment it could be reversed by an infinitesimal change. It proceeds infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, with the system and surroundings always in near-equilibrium.

All other processes are irreversible.
points: Reversible: infinitely slow, a series of equilibrium states, reversible by an infinitesimal change.
On a p–V graph, reversible compression needs the least work and reversible expansion gives the most work.

questions.q: A reversible process is one which:
o: Proceeds infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states
Can be reversed only by a large change
questions.e: NCERT: a reversible process proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states and can be reversed by an infinitesimal change.

questions.q: For the same initial and final volumes, the magnitude of work done BY a gas on isothermal expansion is maximum when the expansion is:
questions.e: In reversible expansion, p_ex tracks the gas pressure, giving the largest area under the p–V curve.

children.title: Isothermal Reversible Work
children.synopsis:
Under reversible conditions pex = pin ± dp. Since dp·dV is negligible, we can replace pex with the gas pressure p:

wrev = −∫ p dV (Eq. 5.4)

For n mol of ideal gas, p = nRT/V. At constant T (isothermal):

wrev = −nRT ln(Vf/Vi) = −2.303 nRT log(Vf/Vi) (Eq. 5.5)

Since p1V1 = p2V2 at constant T, you can also write Vf/Vi = pi/pf.

questions.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas expand isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from 10 L to 100 L. Work done is about (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):
In the expression w_rev = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i), the ratio V_f/V_i can be replaced (isothermal ideal gas) by:
questions.e: Boyle's law: p_i V_i = p_f V_f, so V_f/V_i = p_i/p_f.

children.title: Free Expansion
children.synopsis:
Expansion of a gas into vacuum (pex = 0) is free expansion. No work is done, whether the process is reversible or irreversible.

For an ideal gas expanding isothermally into vacuum, Joule found experimentally that q = 0 as well. So ΔU = 0.

NCERT Problem 5.2: 2 L of gas at 10 atm expands isothermally into vacuum to 10 L. Then q = −w = 0 × 8 = 0: no work and no heat.
points: Ideal gas, isothermal free expansion: q = 0, w = 0, ΔU = 0.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally into vacuum. Which is correct?
questions.e: Against zero external pressure, w = 0. For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0, so q = 0 too.

children.title: q and w for Different Processes
children.synopsis:
Put w = −pexΔV into the First Law: ΔU = q − pexΔV.

ProcessResult
Constant volume (ΔV = 0)ΔU = qV
Isothermal irreversible (ideal gas, ΔU = 0)q = −w = pex(Vf − Vi)
Isothermal reversible (ideal gas)q = −w = 2.303 nRT log(Vf/Vi)
Adiabaticq = 0, ΔU = wad

NCERT trio for one expansion (2 L → 10 L, 25 °C):

  • Into vacuum: q = 0
  • Against 1 atm: q = 8 L atm
  • Reversible, 1 mol: q ≈ 39.4 L atm

The same initial and final states give different q and w on different paths, a direct demonstration that q and w are path functions.

questions.q: For an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which statement is correct?
questions.e: For an ideal gas, U depends only on T. Isothermal means ΔU = 0, so q = −w.

questions.q: Heat absorbed at constant volume equals:
questions.e: At constant volume no pV work is done, so ΔU = q_V.

children.title: 5.2.2 Enthalpy (H)
children.synopsis: Most reactions run at constant pressure (open flasks, test tubes), not constant volume. So we define a state function whose change equals the heat at constant pressure: enthalpy, H = U + pV. This sub-topic also covers extensive vs intensive properties, heat capacity, and Cp − CV = R.

children.title: (a) H = U + pV and ΔH = q(p)
children.synopsis:
At constant pressure: ΔU = qp − pΔV. Rearranging gives qp = (U2 + pV2) − (U1 + pV1). This motivates:

H = U + pV (Eq. 5.7) so qp = ΔH

The word comes from the Greek enthalpien, 'to warm' or 'heat content'.

  • H depends on U, p and V, which are all state functions, so H is a state function.
  • Therefore qp is path-independent, even though q in general is not.
  • At constant p: ΔH = ΔU + pΔV (Eq. 5.8).
  • At constant V: ΔH = ΔU = qV.

Sign: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (heat released) and positive for endothermic reactions (heat absorbed).
traps: q is path-dependent in general, but q_p (= ΔH) and q_V (= ΔU) are path-independent.

questions.q: Heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure is equal to:
questions.e: By definition, ΔH = q_p.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction:
questions.e: Exothermic reactions release heat, so ΔH is negative.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
o: q_p is path-independent because it equals ΔH
questions.e: H is a state function, so ΔH, and hence q_p, does not depend on path.

children.title: ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT
children.synopsis:
For solids and liquids, the volume change is tiny, so ΔH ≈ ΔU. With gases the difference matters.

At constant p and T, pVA = nART and pVB = nBRT, so pΔV = ΔngRT. This gives:

ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT (Eq. 5.10)

Δng = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. Ignore solids and liquids.

ΔngRelation
> 0ΔH > ΔU
= 0ΔH = ΔU
< 0ΔH < ΔU

NCERT Problem 5.5: vaporising 1 mol of water at 100 °C, ΔH = 41 kJ mol⁻¹ and Δng = 1. So ΔU = 41 − (8.3 × 373 × 10⁻³) ≈ 37.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
traps: Count only GASEOUS species for Δn_g. In CH₄ combustion water is liquid, so Δn_g = 1 − 3 = −2.
Use R in kJ (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) when ΔH is in kJ.

questions.q: For CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔU = −X kJ mol⁻¹. Then ΔH is:
questions.e: Δn_g = 1 − 3 = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT, which is less than ΔU.

questions.q: For which reaction is ΔH = ΔU?
questions.e: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.

questions.q: ΔvapH of water at 373 K is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔvapU (water vapour as ideal gas) is about:
For C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) at 298 K, Δn_g is:
questions.e: Gaseous products 3, gaseous reactants 6, so Δn_g = −3. Liquid water is not counted.

children.title: (b) Extensive & Intensive Properties
children.synopsis:
Extensive: the value depends on the amount of matter. Examples: mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity (also entropy and Gibbs energy).

Intensive: the value does not depend on amount. Examples: temperature, pressure, density.

Molar property χm = χ/n, an extensive property per mole. It is intensive. Examples: molar volume Vm and molar heat capacity Cm.

NCERT test (Fig 5.6): split a gas (V, T) in half with a partition. Each half has volume V/2 but the same T. So V is extensive and T is intensive.
points: Ratio of two extensive properties = intensive (density = m/V; C_m = C/n).
traps: Heat capacity is EXTENSIVE, but specific heat and molar heat capacity are INTENSIVE.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.e: Molar heat capacity = C/n, the ratio of two extensive quantities, so it is intensive.

questions.q: Which set contains only extensive properties?
questions.e: Mass, volume and enthalpy all scale with the amount of substance.

children.title: (c) Heat Capacity
children.synopsis:
Heat absorbed shows up as a temperature rise: q = C ΔT, where C is the heat capacity. Its magnitude depends on the size, composition and nature of the system.

  • Large C, small temperature rise for a given heat. Water has a large heat capacity.
  • Molar heat capacity Cm = C/n: heat to raise 1 mol by 1 °C (1 K).
  • Specific heat (capacity) c: heat to raise unit mass by 1 °C (1 K).

q = c × m × ΔT = C ΔT (Eq. 5.11)

questions.q: Heat needed to raise the temperature of 60.0 g of Al from 35 °C to 55 °C (molar heat capacity 24 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, M = 27 g mol⁻¹) is about:
A substance with a large heat capacity will show:
o: A large temperature rise for a given heat input
A small temperature rise for a given heat input
questions.e: q = CΔT, so for fixed q, a larger C gives a smaller ΔT.

children.title: (d) Cp − Cv = R (Ideal Gas)
children.synopsis:
qV = CVΔT = ΔU and qp = CpΔT = ΔH.

For 1 mol of ideal gas, ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) = ΔU + Δ(RT) = ΔU + RΔT. Substituting:

CpΔT = CVΔT + RΔT ⟹ Cp − CV = R (Eq. 5.13)

So Cp > CV always. At constant pressure, part of the heat goes into expansion work.

Useful extra (from the NCERT box in 5.5): for a monoatomic gas, CV = 3/2 R and Cp = 5/2 R.

questions.q: For one mole of an ideal gas, Cp − Cv equals:
questions.e: From ΔH = ΔU + RΔT for 1 mol of ideal gas, Cp − Cv = R.

questions.q: Why is Cp greater than Cv for a gas?
o: At constant pressure, part of the heat is used to do expansion work
At constant volume, heat is lost
questions.e: At constant p, the gas expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same ΔT.

title: 5.3 Measuring ΔU and ΔH: Calorimetry
synopsis: Calorimetry measures heat changes. The process runs in a calorimeter immersed in a known volume of liquid. Knowing the heat capacities of the liquid and the calorimeter, the measured temperature change gives the heat. There are two set-ups: constant volume (gives ΔU) and constant pressure (gives ΔH).

children.title: (a) ΔU: Bomb Calorimeter
children.synopsis:
A sealed steel vessel (the bomb) sits in a water bath, so no heat is lost to the surroundings. The substance burns in pure dioxygen inside the bomb. The heat released passes into the water, and its temperature is monitored.

  • The bomb is sealed, so volume is constant. No work is done, even for reactions involving gases (ΔV = 0).
  • The heat measured is qV = ΔU. It comes from ΔT and the known heat capacity of the calorimeter (q = CΔT).

questions.q: A bomb calorimeter measures:
questions.e: The bomb is sealed and rigid (ΔV = 0), so the heat measured is q_V = ΔU.

questions.q: Why is no work done in a bomb calorimeter even when gases are produced?
o: The volume of the sealed bomb is constant
questions.e: w = −pΔV and ΔV = 0 in the sealed steel bomb.

children.title: (b) ΔH: Constant-pressure Calorimeter
children.synopsis:
Heat changes at constant (atmospheric) pressure are measured in an open calorimeter (Fig 5.8). Since ΔH = qp, the heat measured is the heat of reaction, or enthalpy of reaction, ΔrH.

  • Exothermic: heat evolved, qp < 0, ΔrH < 0
  • Endothermic: heat absorbed, qp > 0, ΔrH > 0

questions.q: The heat absorbed or evolved at constant pressure in a calorimeter is called:
questions.e: q_p = Δ_rH, the enthalpy (heat) of reaction.

children.title: Worked: Burning Graphite in a Bomb
children.synopsis:
1 g of graphite burns in a bomb calorimeter (CV = 20.7 kJ K⁻¹), and the temperature rises from 298 K to 299 K.

  1. Heat gained by the calorimeter = 20.7 × 1 = 20.7 kJ. The reaction lost the same amount, so q = −20.7 kJ per gram.
  2. Per mole (12 g): ΔU = 12 × (−20.7) = −2.48 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹.
  3. C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) has Δng = 1 − 1 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.

NCERT erratum: the text writes ΔU for 1 g as '−20.7 kJ K⁻¹'. The correct unit is kJ (it is an energy, not a heat capacity).

questions.q: A reaction in a bomb calorimeter (heat capacity 10.0 kJ K⁻¹) raises the temperature by 2.0 K. q for the reaction is:
questions.e: The calorimeter gains CΔT = 20 kJ. The reaction lost it, so q = −20 kJ (exothermic).

questions.q: For C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), the relation between ΔH and ΔU is:
questions.e: Δn_g = 1 − 1 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.
